key_insight: Language models can use self-generated samples from their own training distribution as replay data to nearly eliminate catastrophic forgetting; residual forgetting occurs primarily when model capacity or optimization constraints are insufficient.
problem_solved: Reducing catastrophic forgetting in continual learning for language models without requiring storage or access to original training exemplars.
method: Let the model sample (self-generate) prior-task examples from its own learned distribution and use those samples as replay data during new-task training.
Mix self-generated replay with new-task training (controlled sampling/temperature and weighting) to preserve prior-task performance while learning new tasks.
Empirically analyze when self-replay succeeds or fails by varying model capacity and optimization settings (scaling, ablations, retention metrics).
impact: Enables practical, privacy-friendly continual learning for language models by removing the need to store past data; highlights that sufficient model capacity and proper optimization remain critical to fully prevent forgetting.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing retention (performance on prior tasks): no replay vs stored-exemplar replay vs self-generated replay
Pipeline diagram: model → self-generate samples → mix with new-task data → update model (replay loop)
Line/curve plot of model capacity (size or remaining capacity) vs amount of forgetting to show threshold effects
Heatmap or table of ablation results showing impact of optimization settings (learning rate, replay ratio, temperature) on forgetting
paper_title: Forgetting in Language Models: Capacity, Optimization, and Self-Generated Replay
paper_authors: Martin Marek, Dongkyu Cho, Shikai Qiu, Rumi Chunara, Pavel Izmailov
